To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the methanogenic community in stable cellulolytic cultures is dominated by Methanosarcinacea at 30°C, whereas Methanosaetacea dominate at 15°C.
the archaeal communities of two cellulose-methanogenic enrichment cultures at two temperatures (15 and/or 30°C) were different, but the temperature optima for the CH4 production were the same.

(i) a novel lineage of Methanomicrobiales was identified in rice soil, (ii) the methanogenic activity was dominated by the novel lineage in an enrichment culture from the rice soil, but (iii) further transfers of the culture resulted in the dominance by Methanosarcinacaea at 30 and Methanosaetaaceae at 15°C.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the establishment of a cellulose-degrading methanogenic culture, which is dominated by a novel lineage of Euryarchaeotes, and its adaptation to different growth temperatures.
the establishment of stable methanogenic cellulose-degrading cultures and the analysis of the archaeal communities in these cultures at 15°C and 30°C.
the structure and function of a methanogenic archaea community in a stable cellulose-degradating enrichment culture, which was established by a long-term cultivation of a soil sample.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the archaeal community structure and function are not necessarily linked.
the archaeal communities of the stable cellulose-decomposing cultures were different at the two different incubation temperatures but their functions were very similar.
the archaeal community in the rice soil is not only dominated by Methanosarcinacea and Methanosaeta, but also by ‘rice cluster I’.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a stable cellulose-decomposing methanogenic culture can be established at 15°C with the same archaeal community as at 30°C.
the archaeal community in the cellulose-degrading cultures was highly adaptable and that the archaeal communities were not necessarily adapted to the temperature of the environment.

the methanogenic cellulose degradation in the rice field soil is performed by a complex archaeal community, but the dominant methanogens in this community are not necessarily the same at different temperatures.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the temperature optimum is not a good indicator of community composition.
the archaeal communities in the cellulose-degrading cultures were dominated by different archaeal lineages after adaptation to different temperatures.
the archaeal community structure is not the only determinant of the optimal temperature for methanogenesis from cellulose.
